title: Superconducting chip claim: don't change the process node, change the temperature zone — 28nm logic can hit 5nm performance
dek: Move logic into the liquid-helium temperature zone and replace transistors with superconducting switches: that's Snowcap's bet — tape out RISC-V first, then claim 28nm-class logic can deliver 5nm-class performance.
why: If you're watching the compute power wall, this episode offers a third route — don't squeeze transistors, move the whole logic stack into the liquid-helium temperature zone; a former Intel CEO has already placed a bet. The risks and the numbers are both on the table, so it's worth a listen.
who: Hard-tech investors trying to verify whether superconducting computing is a route or a story, plus CPU and supercomputer architects studying the chip power wall.
skip: Anyone already familiar with overclocking and liquid-nitrogen cooling can skip the 0:00-2:01 overclocking preamble.

points.h: The ceiling on extreme overclocking is heat removal, not the chip
points.body: This episode opens from the overclocking industry: everyday chips rely on air cooling, higher-power ones use water cooling, and beyond that you need sub-zero media like dry ice and liquid nitrogen. Extreme overclockers raise voltage to chase the highest frequencies, the chip gets hotter and hotter, and the only way out is ever more extreme cooling. The host says he was an extreme overclocker himself and once held the world number two spot — though it only lasted a day and a half. His key reference point: that kind of overclocking exists just to run a benchmark for a few minutes at 8.5GHz, whereas real superconducting computing is not chasing an instantaneous record but logic at near-zero power.

points.h: In liquid-helium overclocking the expensive part isn't the helium, it's the transfer line
points.body: Going from liquid nitrogen to liquid helium, physics starts to interfere. Liquid helium costs roughly 20 times as much as liquid nitrogen (liquid nitrogen is about a dollar a liter), but that isn't the main expense: getting liquid helium from a large storage tank into a 3-4 kilogram copper overclocking pot through the transfer line costs 5000 dollars per single use. Both Intel and Asus have done liquid-helium overclocking, and records have broken past 9GHz. The host warns that when temperatures drop this far, material behavior changes drastically — some platforms have a ‘cold bug’ where the system simply won't boot below a certain temperature; only platforms without a cold bug are suitable for liquid-helium play.

points.h: The lure of superconductivity isn't faster, it's zero resistance
points.body: Overclocking is about squeezing frequencies out of existing materials; superconductivity is a different story: electrons flow through a superconducting material with no resistance, which amounts to free transport. The vast majority of superconductors today require extremely low temperatures, and room-temperature superconductivity is still stuck in a state of research back-and-forth. The key inference here: if an entire chip's switching logic could operate in the superconducting state, energy per operation would be ‘orders of magnitude’ better than today's laptops. The host deliberately states it fully and then pulls back — superconductivity is still the holy grail, not yet in hand. This sets up Snowcap's entrance later.

points.h: What the former Intel CEO bet on is the temperature zone, not the process node
points.body: Snowcap Compute just closed a seed round, with former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger sitting on its board. Their bet is that they can build superconducting chips that operate at roughly 4-15K, the liquid-helium temperature zone. Structurally it's no longer billions of transistors but a new kind of switch that works at superconducting temperatures — the Josephson junction. At this stage Snowcap's goal is to first build a RISC-V-class CPU at cryogenic temperatures, getting power consumption close to free; the price is that the whole machine must stay in the liquid-helium temperature zone, and the cooling itself consumes energy.

points.h: The new variable in superconducting logic is fitting into standard EDA flows
points.body: There is no shortage of long-term researchers: a US defense contractor built chips integrating tens of millions of Josephson junctions, IMEC reached hundreds of millions, and built accompanying logic and EDA tools. Snowcap's differentiator is compatibility: they say this kind of superconducting logic can go into standard EDA flows and can be taped out on ordinary CMOS processes, with niobium titanium nitride as the material. The core conclusion the host takes away: the efficiency advantage from superconductivity is equivalent to achieving near-5nm chip performance with 28nm logic — note this is not a smaller process node but the equivalent gain from lower power.

points.h: Cryo CMOS is only an intermediate state; the real hurdle is scale
points.body: Snowcap plans to deliver its first chip in 2026, followed by a deployable RISC-V design. For the intermediate state, look at cryo CMOS: it runs in the roughly 72-77K liquid-nitrogen zone, and although it isn't superconducting, the low temperature itself pushes power down. The real hurdle to cross is going from cryo CMOS into superconductivity; the host's doubt about this is ‘can you scale it up at high performance’ — being able to run and being able to commercialize at scale are two different things.

points.h: Cold booting is nothing new; the hard part is keeping the whole machine in liquid helium
points.body: This segment provides a real-world footnote on cryogenic tape-out: AMD's first Zen 1 A0 sample, which came out when the company was most short of money, could only boot at dry-ice sub-zero temperatures because of a design flaw, and was later fixed to run at room temperature. So low temperatures in testing and boot are nothing unusual; but keeping an entire processor in the liquid-helium temperature zone is an infrastructure problem, including helium supply — liquid helium is also the lifeblood of the superconducting magnets in MRI machines, and there was a helium shortage a few years ago.

points.h: Snowcap doesn't sell IP; it sells a closed all-in-one machine
points.body: Snowcap positions itself not as selling IP but as delivering a complete system. The host's judgment is that precisely because of the infrastructure barrier of the liquid-helium temperature zone, the product form will be a nearly closed all-in-one machine, with the software stack rebuilt from scratch. A seed-stage company still has A/B/C rounds ahead of it; still, they have already brought in advisors and former employees with Apple, Nvidia and Google backgrounds. On this topic, it's worth staying skeptical and worth following.

The main cost is actually the tube you need to get it from this massive compressed gas sewer into your massive 3-4 kilogram copper pot. That tube, single use, is five grand.

When you go down to those cold temperatures, the way the materials work is incredibly different. In some chips and in some platforms, you might experience what's called a cold bug. It gets too cold for the system to boot or to work.

There has been a strong effort to make room temperature semiconductors. We're not there yet. Research, if you follow that area, sometimes stalls and sometimes there's a breakthrough. If that happens, one day we may have free energy. Right now, we don't. Right now, superconducting is the holy grail.

But what if you could make a chip that was superconducting? Suddenly, you now have a processor that can do compute for next to no energy. And we're talking orders of magnitude better energy consumption per operation than this laptop, for example.
